📧 Task 4 · Email Spam Detection with Machine Learning¶

Objective: Build an NLP binary classifier that separates spam messages from legitimate (ham) messages.

Tech stack: Python · pandas · scikit-learn (TF-IDF, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM) · NLTK · re · matplotlib/seaborn · WordCloud · Jupyter Notebook

Dataset: SMS Spam Collection (UCI ML Repository / Kaggle) — 5,572 English messages labelled ham or spam.

Download spam.csv from Kaggle and place it in the data/ folder next to this notebook.

Notebook outline¶

  1. Setup & imports
  2. Data loading & cleaning
  3. Class distribution (spam vs ham)
  4. Text preprocessing pipeline

Observations

  • The dataset is imbalanced: roughly 87% ham vs 13% spam. Accuracy alone can be misleading — a model that always predicts "ham" would already score ~87%. So precision, recall and F1 for the spam class are the metrics that matter.
  • Spam messages are noticeably longer on average (they pack in offers, numbers, links and calls to action).

4. Text Preprocessing Pipeline¶

Each message goes through these steps:

Step What it does Example
1. Lowercase Treats "FREE" and "free" as the same word FREE Entry → free entry
2. Remove URLs & numbers Replaces them with tokens url / num instead of losing the signal entirely call 08712 → call num
3. Remove punctuation Strips !, ?, £, . etc. win!!! → win
4. Remove stopwords Drops very common words with little meaning (the, is, and) you have won → won
5. Stemming (Porter) Reduces words to their root winning, winner → win

Replacing numbers and URLs with tokens (instead of deleting them) is deliberate: phone numbers and links are among the strongest spam signals.

In [9]:
stop_words = set(stopwords.words("english"))
stemmer = PorterStemmer()

def preprocess(text: str) -> str:
    """Clean one message: lowercase -> URLs/numbers -> punctuation -> stopwords -> stemming."""
    text = text.lower()                                              # 1. lowercase
    text = re.sub(r"(https?://\S+|www\.\S+)", " url ", text)          # 2a. URLs -> 'url'
    text = re.sub(r"\d+", " num ", text)                              # 2b. numbers -> 'num'
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans(string.punctuation, " " * len(string.punctuation)))  # 3. punctuation
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", " ", text)                             #    leftover symbols (e.g. £)
    tokens = [w for w in text.split() if w not in stop_words and len(w) > 1]  # 4. stopwords
    tokens = [stemmer.stem(w) for w in tokens]                         # 5. stemming
    return " ".join(tokens)

# Show the pipeline on one real spam message
sample = df.loc[df["label"] == "spam", "message"].iloc[0]
print("BEFORE:", sample)
print("AFTER :", preprocess(sample))

7. Feature Extraction with TF-IDF¶

What does TF-IDF measure?¶

TF-IDF (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency) gives each word in a message a weight that reflects how important that word is to that message, relative to the whole collection.

  • TF (Term Frequency) — how often word t appears in message d. More occurrences → more important to that message. $$TF(t, d) = \frac{\text{count of } t \text{ in } d}{\text{total words in } d}$$
  • IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) — how rare the word is across all messages. Words found everywhere (go, ok) get a low IDF; rare, distinctive words (prize, claim) get a high IDF. $$IDF(t) = \log\frac{1 + N}{1 + DF(t)} + 1 \quad (\text{scikit-learn's smoothed form; } N = \text{no. of messages, } DF = \text{messages containing } t)$$
  • TF-IDF = TF × IDF → a word scores high only when it is frequent in this message but rare overall.

Why it suits spam detection: words like "prize" or "claim" are rare in normal chat but common in spam, so TF-IDF highlights exactly those words, while down-weighting filler that appears in every message. Each message becomes a numeric vector the classifier can learn from.

Mnemonic: TF = "kitna baar is message mein", IDF = "kitna rare poore dataset mein".

Settings used: ngram_range=(1, 2) (single words + two-word phrases like "call num"), min_df=2 (ignore words seen only once), sublinear_tf=True (log-scale repeated words). The vectorizer is fitted on training data only to avoid data leakage.

In [14]:
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True)

X_train_tfidf = tfidf.fit_transform(X_train)   # learn vocabulary + IDF from TRAIN only
X_test_tfidf  = tfidf.transform(X_test)        # reuse it on TEST

print("TF-IDF matrix (train):", X_train_tfidf.shape)
print("TF-IDF matrix (test) :", X_test_tfidf.shape)
print("Vocabulary size      :", len(tfidf.vocabulary_))

8. Model Training¶

Model Why
Multinomial Naive Bayes Industry standard for text: fast, works with word-frequency features, strong baseline
Logistic Regression Linear, interpretable; class_weight="balanced" compensates for the 87/13 imbalance
Linear SVM Usually the strongest linear text classifier on sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF data
In [16]:
models = {
    "Multinomial Naive Bayes": MultinomialNB(alpha=0.1),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=10, class_weight="balanced",
                                              random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Linear SVM": LinearSVC(C=1.0, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}

predictions = {}
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
    predictions[name] = model.predict(X_test_tfidf)
    print(f"✔ Trained: {name}")

✔ Trained: Multinomial Naive Bayes
✔ Trained: Logistic Regression

10. Discussion — Why is recall particularly important for spam detection?¶

Recall (for the spam class) = of all the messages that really are spam, what fraction did the model catch? $$\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

Why it matters here:

  1. Missed spam is the main failure the filter exists to prevent. Every False Negative is a spam/phishing message landing in the inbox. Spam often carries scams, phishing links or malware, so a single missed message can lead to a stolen password or financial fraud.
  2. Imbalanced data hides poor recall. With ~87% ham, a model can show 95%+ accuracy while still letting through a large share of spam. Recall exposes this directly; accuracy doesn't.
  3. Spam arrives at scale. Even 10% missed spam means thousands of junk/scam messages for a large mail provider every day.

But recall is not everything — the precision trade-off:

  • A False Positive (genuine email sent to the spam folder) can also be costly — e.g. a missed job offer or OTP. So real systems aim for high recall without sacrificing precision, which is why F1-score (their harmonic mean) is used to pick a balanced model.
  • In practice, recall can be tuned by lowering the decision threshold, and users can still check the spam folder for the occasional false positive — whereas a missed scam may already have done its damage.

Exam one-liner: Spam detection mein recall important hai kyunki har missed spam (False Negative) ek potential phishing/scam hai jo inbox tak pahunch jaata hai; imbalanced data mein high accuracy ke peeche low recall chhup sakta hai.

11. Best Model¶

In [21]:
# Pick the model with the highest F1 on spam (balances recall and precision)
best_name = results["F1 (spam)"].idxmax()
print(f"🏆 Best model: {best_name}")
print(results.loc[best_name].round(4).to_string())

🏆 Best model: Logistic Regression
Accuracy            0.9874
Precision (spam)    0.9609
Recall (spam)       0.9389
F1 (spam)           0.9498

🏆 Best model: Logistic Regression (TF-IDF, class_weight="balanced")

Model Accuracy Precision (spam) Recall (spam) F1 (spam) Missed spam (FN) Ham flagged (FP)
Multinomial NB 98.45% 96.75% 90.84% 93.70% 12 4
Logistic Regression 98.74% 96.09% 93.89% 94.98% 8 5
Linear SVM 98.65% 96.06% 93.13% 94.57% 9 5

Justification

  1. Highest spam recall (93.9%) — it misses only 8 of 131 spam messages, vs 12 for Naive Bayes. Since recall is the priority in spam detection (Section 10), this is the deciding factor.
  2. Highest F1-score (0.950) — the gain in recall costs just one extra false positive compared with Naive Bayes, so precision stays high (96.1%).
  3. Highest overall accuracy (98.7%).
  4. class_weight="balanced" makes the model pay more attention to the minority spam class, which directly helps recall on this imbalanced dataset.

Note on Naive Bayes: it remains an excellent baseline — the highest precision (fewest genuine messages wrongly flagged) and the fastest to train. If wrongly blocking a genuine email were the bigger worry, NB would be a reasonable choice. Linear SVM is a very close second overall.

Sample predictions on new messages¶

In [22]:
best_model = models[best_name]

new_messages = [
    "Congratulations! You've WON a £1000 Walmart gift card. Call 09061701461 now to claim your prize!",
    "Hey, are we still meeting for lunch tomorrow at 1?",
    "URGENT: Your account has been suspended. Verify at http://secure-login.example.com within 24 hrs",
    "Can you send me the notes from today's class? Thanks bro",
    "FREE entry into our weekly draw! Text WIN to 80086 to receive your free ringtone",
]

def predict(messages):
    """Run raw text through the SAME preprocessing + TF-IDF used in training, then classify."""
    vec = tfidf.transform([preprocess(m) for m in messages])
    return ["SPAM 🚫" if p == 1 else "HAM ✅" for p in best_model.predict(vec)]

pd.DataFrame({"message": new_messages, "prediction": predict(new_messages)})

12. Conclusion¶

  • The SMS Spam Collection was loaded, de-duplicated and found to be imbalanced (~87% ham / 13% spam), so precision/recall/F1 on the spam class were used instead of accuracy alone.
  • A text preprocessing pipeline (lowercase → URL/number tokens → punctuation removal → stopword removal → Porter stemming) was applied, and messages were converted to TF-IDF vectors (unigrams + bigrams).
  • Three classifiers were trained: Multinomial Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression and Linear SVM. All exceeded 97% accuracy; the differences show up mainly in spam recall.
  • WordClouds confirmed that spam is driven by action/reward words (call, free, claim, prize, txt) and phone numbers.
  • Logistic Regression is the best model: 98.7% accuracy, 93.9% spam recall and the highest F1 (0.950), missing only 8 of 131 spam messages. Naive Bayes had the highest precision.

Possible extensions: tune hyperparameters with GridSearchCV, adjust the decision threshold to push recall higher, try lemmatization instead of stemming, or save the model + vectorizer with joblib and serve it through a small Flask/Streamlit app.
